entries.title: NCAA still weighing expanding March Madness to 76 teams
entries.summary: <p>The NCAA is still deliberating expanding March Madness on both the men's and women's sides to 76 teams for next season — a much-expected development that's been in the works for years.</p><p>The NCAA released a brief statement Tuesday in the wake of an ESPN report that cited unnamed sources saying a decision to add eight teams to the bracket is a mere formality that's expected in May.</p><p>"Expanding the basketball tournaments would require approval from multiple NCAA committees, including the men's and women's basketball committees, and no final recommendations or decisions have been made at this time," the statement said.</p><p>Earlier this month at the Final Four, NCAA President Charlie Baker said the committees would, in fact, return to discussing the expansion once this year's tournament was over.</p><p>The tournaments have been at 68 teams since 2011, when four play-in games were added to the beginning of the first week of play. The new format would add eight more at-large teams and take eight more teams out of the main bracket for play-in games.</p><p>The expansion isn't expected to generate a lot more income because it will only add games early in the first week. The current TV deal runs through 2032 and could be tweaked slightly.</p><p>Regardless of finances, the expansion would give power conferences more chances to place teams in the bracket — a growing concern as those conferences seek more power and control over college sports in the era of name, image and likeness compensation and the transfer portal.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox loving Munetaka Murakami’s home run bonanza, but striving for balance on offense
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> completed their late rally in a midnight comeback win against the Angels on Monday the way they have racked up most of their runs early this season: with the long ball.</p><p>No one on the South Side will ever complain about a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/28/chicago-white-sox-los-angeles-angels-murakami-munetaka-miguel-vargas-tristan-peters-osvaldo-bido-grant-taylor-bryan-hudson-will-venable-rain-delay-dog-day" target="_blank" ><u>go-ahead</u></a>, three-run home run from rookie sensation Munetaka Murakami, who entered play Tuesday with an MLB-high 12 home runs in his first month.</p><p>Nor will anyone turn up their nose at third baseman Miguel Vargas going back-to-back with Murakami for his sixth homer of the year for some needed insurance, just a week after they made it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/21/munetaka-murakami-homer-four-straight-games-white-sox-arizona" target="_blank" ><u>three in a row</u></a> along with fellow infield slugger Colson Montgomery.</p><p>But to stay within a surprising three games of first place in the American League Central, the Sox will likely need to diversify an offense that has generated more than half its runs the long way early in the year, according to Baseball Prospectus. The Sox entered play with 35 home runs on the season, good for ninth in baseball, while their run total of 121 sat 21st.</p><p>Manager Will Venable said his squad is proving that when they’re executing, they can generate runs however they need to — and in modern baseball, that includes a healthy dose of dingers.</p><p>“The long ball is great, and we've certainly benefited. And when we hit home runs and multiple home runs, we probably are winning those games,” Venable said. “At the same time, there's been a lot of other things that these guys are doing well, specifically at the bottom of the order, with the situational hitting, the bunting, being aggressive on the bases. And for us as an offense, that's what it's going to take.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">MUNE AT MIDNIGHT! 🤯 <a href="https://t.co/yrE0mWKsM0">pic.twitter.com/yrE0mWKsM0</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://twitter.com/whitesox/status/2048988297041473778?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 28, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The situational hits <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/26/chicago-white-sox-washington-nationals-will-venable-sean-burke-munetaka-murakami-seranthony-dominguez" target="_blank" ><u>were lacking</u></a> in the Sox’ weekend series against the Nationals, scoring nine runs in three games that included two extra-inning losses, underscoring the hot-and-cold nature of their bats after exploding for 22 in Arizona to close out <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/23/munetaka-murakami-home-run-streak-andrew-benintendi-white-sox-win-arizona" target="_blank" ><u>a high-octane West Coast road trip</u></a>.</p><p>Their 25 home runs from April 12-27 were third-most in baseball, thanks in no small part to Murakami’s five-game home run streak that has him accounting for a third of the team’s total. His .965 OPS has also buoyed a team offense of .692 that ranked 21st in MLB.</p><p>“We do need the slug. Everyone needs that slug. At the same time, you've got to find production throughout your order and throughout your lineup, and find different ways to get guys on base and score,” said Venable, who’s also had the Sox thinking small. Their 24 bunt attempts were the most in baseball as of Tuesday.</p><p>“We’re gonna have to use that tool. We’re gonna value that tool, just as anything else,” Sox hitting coach Derek Shomon said over the weekend. “We absolutely have to practice that, and the guys have done that.”</p><p>Shomon called it a “multifaceted offense when this thing’s firing off on all cylinders.”</p><p>“We have guys that can slug, we have guys that can move the baseball forward, we have guys that can and will lay down a bunt. That’s cool, it’s not just a one-trick pony, even though some nights it feels like it is. When it is firing off, there’s a lot of different solutions to score runs,” he said.</p><p>Second baseman Chase Meidroth, who clubbed a leadoff home run for the Sox on Opening Day and has dropped four bunts since then, tipped his cap to the heart-of-the-order power from Murakami, Vargas and Montgomery, who hit his eighth homer early in Tuesday's game. </p><p>“There’s a lot of ways to win a baseball game. Whether it’s small ball or the long ball, stringing together good at-bats, there are a lot of different ways to win a baseball game,” Meidroth said. “Those three guys have done a great job of hitting the long ball. As much as we can get those guys up with runners in scoring position, it’s what we are going to do right now.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Brown's Olivia Pichardo, the first woman to pitch a college game, keeps focus on baseball
entries.summary: <p>In her ideal world, Olivia Pichardo would just play ball and not take attention away from her teammates.</p><p>"Sometimes it feels a little ridiculous," she told the Associated Press, "but it's something I understand is going to happen. That's not what my primary focus is ever on."</p><p>Pichardo has grown accustomed to being the only girl on her baseball team during her years in Little League, high school and travel ball. Four years ago she tried out for the Brown University team, made it and early in her freshman season became the first woman to appear in a Division I game when she pinch-hit against Bryant.</p><p>On her senior day last Saturday, she became the first woman to pitch in a Division I game when she got the final out in a key win over Cornell.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">HISTORY: Olivia Pichardo - an <a href="https://twitter.com/MLBDevelops?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@MLBDevelops</a> alum - became the first woman to pitch in a Division I baseball game over the weekend when she came in to shut the door for Brown University against Cornell 👏<br><br>(🎥: <a href="https://twitter.com/espn?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@ESPN</a>)<a href="https://t.co/dUHz2jYYIM">pic.twitter.com/dUHz2jYYIM</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://twitter.com/MLB/status/2049205803697975438?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 28, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>"I feel like sometimes it might distract a bit too much from the success of our team," Pichardo said. "We just made the playoffs for the first time since 2007, so that's a huge accomplishment, and I wouldn't want to take away from that."</p><p>Pichardo was listed as an outfielder and pitcher her first three years and focused only on pitching this season. The fact she stuck it out four years might seem surprising. Brown has played 151 games since Pichardo arrived, and she has appeared in only six. She pinch-hit once as a freshman, once as a sophomore and three times as a junior, when she also played right field for an inning and caught two flies.</p><p>Until Saturday, she hadn't appeared in a game this season, let alone warmed up in the bullpen. With Brown leading Cornell 16-3 in the ninth inning, coach Frank Holbrook's plan was to have little-used reliever Ty Harris get the first two outs and have Pichardo finish.</p><p>The 5-foot-7, 165-pound Pichardo has a four-pitch repertoire that includes a low-80s four-seam fastball to go with a sinker, changeup and curve. She entered with the bases loaded and threw two fastballs to Tyler Beaulieu, who grounded out to short to end Brown's 16-4 win.</p><p>Pichardo said she has never had any problem melding with her teammates. She prefers just being one of the guys and not taking spotlight away from the team. She does, however, understand the magnitude of what she's accomplished, not just in college but also in summer ball. In 2023, she became the first woman to hit a home run in a summer league, connecting for Sag Harbor in the Hamptons Collegiate Baseball League.</p><p>"It's important for inspiring the younger generation of female baseball players, give them some kind of hope, I guess, that if they want to play at the collegiate level, no matter what division, that door is open for them and it is possible," she said.</p><p>Pichardo, who graduates this spring with a degree in business economics, has been able to capitalize on name, image and likeness opportunities as the most visible woman in college baseball. She's in her third year as an endorser for the baseball equipment and apparel company Warstic Sports and she has a deal with Topps Allen & Ginter baseball cards.</p><p>Once Brown's season ends, she'll turn her attention to trying out for the U.S. women's team that will play in the group stage of the 2027 World Cup. She has been a regular on Team USA since 2022 and pitched against Japan in the 2024 World Cup in Thunder Bay, Ontario.</p><p>Pichardo said she's been grateful for every baseball opportunity since her father signed her up for a league in her hometown of Queens, New York, when she was 6.</p><p>"He didn't have any sons, so I like to say I was his designated son," she said. "I've always been able to play at every level that I've progressed to, so there was never any reason for me to stop playing baseball just because I didn't see other women in the same space as me. It was my first sport, my first love and I knew I wanted to try and play at the highest level possible."<br></p>

entries.title: Newcomer Drew Romo’s first two career home runs power White Sox to 5-2 victory vs. Angels
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox were hoping for an offensive jolt at a stagnant position when they designated catcher <b>Reese McGuire</b> for assignment last weekend and recalled <b>Drew Romo</b>, a 24-year-old offseason waiver claim who hit .298/.385/.561 in 17 games at Triple-A Charlotte.</p><p>But they couldn’t have expected what Romo delivered Tuesday against the Angels. He belted the first two home runs of his career — and the first two home runs by a Sox catcher this season.</p><p>The switch-hitting Romo smashed a two-run blast from the left side of the plate against Angels ace <b>Jose Soriano</b> in the fourth inning, then took reliever <b>Brent Suter </b>deep from the right side of the plate in the sixth.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Drew Romo sent that one outta here! <a href="https://t.co/8SEL1qxmTh">pic.twitter.com/8SEL1qxmTh</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://twitter.com/whitesox/status/2049292451790176342?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Romo became the first Sox player to homer from both sides in a game since <b>Leury Garcia</b> did it against the Twins on July 25, 2020.</p><p>‘‘One of the best days of my life,’’ Romo said. ‘‘Everything it has taken to get here, all the ups and downs. Incredible ride, journey.’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Have yourself a night, Drew Romo! 🤯 <a href="https://t.co/d0IaeJ6i9V">pic.twitter.com/d0IaeJ6i9V</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://twitter.com/whitesox/status/2049302724211089473?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>In the second, Soriano had yielded a homer to <b>Colson Montgomery</b>. It was only the second run he had allowed all season.</p><p>‘‘The guy is the best pitcher on the planet right now, and [Romo] put together some really good at-bats,’’ manager <b>Will Venable</b> said.</p><p></p><p>Sox right-hander <b>Davis Martin</b> turned in another solid start, giving up an RBI single to <b>Jo Adell</b> in the fourth and scattering six other hits in 5⅔ innings. He struck out seven and walked one.</p><p></p><p>The Sox had been saddled with a major-league-worst .443 OPS at catcher entering the game, more than 150 points behind the next-worst catching crew in that category. Romo’s breakout boosted that figure to .536.</p><p></p><p>‘‘The teammates have been great,’’ Romo said of his new clubhouse. ‘‘Everyone gets along super-well. I couldn’t ask for a better spot to be in.’’</p><p></p><h3>More outfield pain</h3><p></p><p>Right fielder <b>Everson Pereira</b> left the game with soreness in his right shoulder and is considered day-to-day.</p><p></p><p>Pereira, who spent a week on the injured list earlier this season with a sprained ankle, has provided some much-needed pop in the Sox’ outfield, hitting .250/.310/.453 with three homers. He’s also a team leader in fun facts as the only player in MLB history with the first name ‘‘Everson.’’</p><p></p><p>Pereira was replaced by <b>Austin Hays</b>, who saw <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/27/white-sox-austin-hays-derek-shomon-will-venable-chris-antonacci-chase-meidroth" target="_blank" >his first action in three weeks</a> after his own IL stint with a pulled hamstring. Hays, who rejoined the team after utility player <b>Tanner Murray</b> suffered an ugly shoulder injury Sunday, went 0-for-2.</p><p></p><h3>Actual moonshot for Mune</h3><p></p><p>The homer <b>Munetaka Murakami</b> golfed out of Rate Field at a 48-degree launch angle Monday was the steepest dinger on record at the ballpark in the Statcast era, which dates to 2015.</p><p></p><p>Only eight other homers ever have made it out of parks at higher angles, according to MLB stathead <b>Sarah Langs</b>.</p><p></p><p>Murakami’s moonshot sailed 101 feet high and 382 feet deep and came off the bat at about 96 mph. It was hardly the prettiest one he has cranked among his major-league-high 12 homers, but it was ‘‘well-timed, for sure,’’ Venable said, and a good example of his effortless power.</p><p></p><p>The ones ‘‘where he’s not getting his ‘A’ swing off and he’s still hitting the ball out of the park are maybe some of the most impressive,’’ Venable said. ‘‘But they’ve all been impressive.’’</p><p></p><h3>Condolences for Cora</h3><p>Venable was as surprised as anyone to see Phillies manager <b>Rob Thomson</b> fired three days after the Red Sox axed <b>Alex Cora</b>. Venable served as Cora’s bench coach with the Red Sox during the 2021-22 seasons.</p><p>‘‘Those guys are two really good guys,’’ Venable said. ‘‘I know Cora really well, having worked for him, and he’s as good a manager as I’ve been around and a special guy. It just kind of speaks to how sensitive these jobs are and these opportunities. It’s tough to see because you care about those guys and you know they’re good guys, but you understand that’s part of baseball.’’</p>

entries.title: Judge under fire for placing suspected Chicago cop killer on home monitoring before Swedish Hospital shooting
entries.summary: <p>Alphanso Talley knows Judge John Lyke Jr. well, having appeared in his courtroom for years.</p><p>In December, Lyke placed Talley, 26, of South Shore on electronic monitoring after the convicted felon was charged with armed carjacking and armed robbery.</p><p>Talley’s now charged with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/27/suspect-charged-in-swedish-hospital-shooting-that-left-1-cop-dead-and-another-fighting-for-his-life-source" target="_blank" >killing a Chicago police officer</a> and wounding another in a bizarre ambush attack at Swedish Hospital on Saturday.</p><p>And Lyke is being blamed for allowing him to previously walk free.</p><p>On Tuesday, they came face to face again for a few brief moments. Talley was supposed to answer for the arrest warrants issued in his cases before Lyke, but the judge punted the hearing to a later date.</p><p>Some officials have seized on Lyke’s decision to grant Talley leniency, saying it exposes the potentially fatal flaws of Cook County’s electronic monitoring program and the state’s cashless bail system.</p><p>Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke’s office had petitioned to keep Talley in custody in the cases before Lyke. On Tuesday, she told reporters the electronic monitoring system was “broken,” insisting that it “is not keeping people safe.”</p><p>“We make sure that we put every bit of information in front of a judge to establish why we believe this person presents a danger, as we did in this case,” O’Neill Burke said. “We established that he had four pending violent felonies, and in spite of that, he was placed on electronic monitoring.”</p><p>Before Saturday’s shooting, Talley stepped into an Albany Park dollar store, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/26/cpd-officer-fatally-shot-john-bartholomew" target="_blank" >snatched a bundle of cash</a> and repeatedly pistol-whipped the clerk, breaking her nose, according to a police report.</p><p>Officers soon tracked Talley to an alley a couple miles away using a GPS device hidden in the stolen money, which was allegedly in his pocket, stained with blood. The arrest report shows the cops also found the victim’s wallet, but not the gun Talley allegedly attacked her with.</p><p>He claimed he’d swallowed bags of drugs, so an ambulance took him on a short but fateful trip to Swedish Hospital, the report says. He was escorted there by cops from the Albany Park District — but not the ones listed in the report as the arresting officers.</p><p>Prosecutors said Talley eventually pulled a gun from under a hospital blanket and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/25/officers-reportedly-injured-shooting-chicago-swedish-hospital-lincoln-square" target="_blank" >shot the two cops</a>, killing 10-year police veteran John Bartholomew and critically wounding the other officer. Talley then shot out a hospital window and fled naked before he was found hiding under a nearby porch, prosecutors said.</p><p>While the robbery report offers new details about the events that led up to the shooting, it’s still unclear how Talley allegedly got the gun past police and into a secure hospital.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> entries.title: Cubs starter Justin Steele's return delayed by elbow strain
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO — More than a year after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> pitcher Justin Steele underwent a second major surgery on his left elbow, new imaging performed Tuesday showed a flexor strain that will delay the 30-year-old left-hander’s comeback beyond the All-Star break, manager Craig Counsell said Tuesday.</p><p>The Cubs had projected this spring that Steele might be back in May or June, but after Steele went Tuesday to see <b>Dr. Keith Meister</b>, the surgeon who performed surgery on Steele last April 18, the flexor strain was detected.</p><p>Counsell said the plan is for Steele to undergo further imaging in a month “to make sure everything is fine.’’ But even if it is determined the flexor strain tendon is healed, it will require further rehabilitation before Steele is able to pitch again for the Cubs, nearly three seasons after his breakout year in 2023, when he went 16-5 with a 3.03 ERA.</p><p>The Cubs already have lost <b>Cade Horton</b> to a season-ending elbow injury after his promising debut last season, and now it is apparent that while the they remain hopeful Steele will return at some point this season, they have no assurance that will occur.</p><p>It is the latest in a tsunami-like wave of pitching injuries for the Cubs, who almost certainly will be in the market for more pitching help. According to an industry source, the Cubs made an offer for <b>Lucas Giolito</b>, but were outbid by the Padres, who signed him last week to a one-year deal with an option that will pay him $3 million this season, with some escalators built in. That contract was far below projections.</p><p>Steele had intended to see Meister for “kind of a final checkup,” Counsell said, but after throwing a bullpen last weekend in Arizona, reported discomfort.</p><p>“I think more than anything it’s frustrating for Justin,’’ Counsell said. “During the course of these rehabs, there are always good days and bad days that you navigate through. But just when you start getting back to where Justin was, and getting fairly close to getting back into competition . . . unfortunately we’ve hit another speed bump, and it’s going to take longer.’’</p><p>Steele underwent conventional Tommy John surgery on his ulnar collateral ligament in 2017, his third season in pro ball. Last year, he underwent an innovative procedure developed by Meister that incorporated a tendon graft reinforced with a UCL brace — a collagen-coated tape.</p><p><b>Not a steal</b></p><p>Cubs catcher <b>Miguel Amaya</b> still does not have a stolen base to his name in the major leagues. His advance to second base Saturday in L.A. after being hit by a pitch by the Dodgers’ <b>Roki Sasaki</b> was scored a wild pitch, rather than a stolen base. It still prompted Dodgers’ catcher <b>Dalton Rushing</b> to mutter, “Fat [expletive].”</p><p>For the record, Amaya this season ranks 37th among catchers in sprint speed (minimum 10 opportunities) at 25 feet per second, according to Baseball Savant.</p><p>He ranks 337th among all players. <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> checks in as the fastest Cubs baserunner at 29.1 feet per second, just ahead of <b>Matt Shaw </b>(28.9). Amaya has never attempted a stolen base in the big leagues, but stole 16 bases in 19 minor-league attempts.</p><p><b>Notes</b></p><p><b>Alex Bregman</b>, who fouled a ball off his foot Sunday, was given the day off after playing in the season’s first 29 games. Shaw played third. Shaw already has made starts at four positions this season — first base, second base, third base and center field — and entered as a defensive replacement in left field Monday night. Sunday was his first big-league start at second base.</p><p>• Counsell said left-handed reliever <b>Riley Martin</b> is expected to be out eight weeks with a strained flexor in his left entries.title: Ex-Park City police officer charged with assaulting woman during traffic stops
entries.summary: <p>A former part-time Park City police officer was charged with repeatedly sexually assaulting a woman during traffic stops, the Park City Police Department said in a statement.</p><p>Patrick Cacho faces charges of aggravated criminal sexual abuse, aggravated battery, official misconduct, and criminal sexual abuse from the Lake County States Attorney’s office, according to the statement. He was arrested by Illinois State Police Tuesday after he was fired from the Park City force earlier in the day.</p><p>The department was notified of the allegations in late January that he “had acted unprofessionally and possibly engaged in criminal conduct while on duty on more than one occasion” over several weeks with a woman during traffic stops, according to the statement.</p><p>The Illinois Law Enforcement Training Standards Board <a class="Link" href="https://www.ptb.illinois.gov/media/1947/2025-12-iletsb-december-board-book.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>waived him from training</u></a> to be reactivated as an officer in September.</p>

entries.title: Chicago drill rapper Lil Zay Osama among six charged by feds in Winnetka home invasion
entries.summary: <p>Chicago drill rapper<b> </b>Lil Zay Osama is among six men facing robbery and kidnapping charges in a federal indictment for their role in a Winnetka home invasion last month in which the intruders allegedly<b> </b>demanded access to a safe, computer and online cryptocurrency<b> </b>accounts.</p><p>U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ office announced the charges Tuesday. A seventh man was arrested Tuesday morning with charges pending,<b> </b>the feds said.</p><p>The charges follow an investigation that involved the FBI, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Winnetka police.</p><p>Prosecutors initially filed charges against three of the men March 23, court records show. A superseding indictment on April 16 added three additional defendants. Osama, 28, who now lives in Los Angeles, was among those charged April 16. His real name is Isaiah<b> </b>Dukes.</p><p>Three Chicago men were also charged. They are Dashun<b> </b>Brown, 24, David<b> </b>Franklin, 24, and Anthony<b> </b>Ramsey, 22. Also facing charges are Khiell<b> </b>Dukes, 30, of Elgin; and Jalen Chambers, 24, of Bourbonnais.</p><p>Documents detailing the allegations against the men remained under seal through Tuesday afternoon. Boutros’ office said the information was sealed while investigators collected evidence to identify additional defendants. The superseding indictment was unsealed Tuesday evening.</p><p>Each defendant has pleaded not guilty. U.S. District Judge Iain Johnston held a hearing<b> </b>Tuesday<b> </b>regarding Osama<b> </b>in Rockford. He and the other five defendants have all been ordered detained. </p><p>The home invasion occurred on March 8. Brown, Ramsey and Franklin were taken into federal custody March 22, prosecutors said. Osama, Dukes and Chambers were taken into custody April 10.</p><p>Prosecutors say Brown posed as a food delivery driver, prompting someone inside the Winnetka home to open the front door. That’s when Brown, Franklin and Chambers allegedly forced their way inside, armed with loaded firearms.</p><p>The feds say two unidentified co-conspirators joined them.</p><p>The intruders allegedly held the victim captive<b> </b>for about an hour and<b> </b>“used firearms to physically restrain the victim,”<b> </b>prosecutors said. They also allegedly demanded access to the safe, computer and the online accounts.</p><p>Eventually, the intruders fled the residence, according to prosecutors. The feds say they then met up with Osama, Dukes, Ramsey and others — who conducted a search to make sure all of the robbery proceeds were collected.</p><p>Osama <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/12/23/family-showered-in-christmas-gifts-after-south-deering-attack-im-so-grateful-for-the-community" target="_blank" >made headlines last December</a> for helping provide Christmas gifts to children <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/11/18/9-year-old-boy-woman-beaten-group-south-deering-attack" target="_blank" >who’d been attacked</a>, along with their mother, in South Deering one month earlier.</p><p>The rapper blamed the attack on kids having too much time on their hands and said “we need positive distractions from the streets.”</p><p>But Osama's also been in trouble with the feds before. A federal judge in Brooklyn <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/usao-edny/pr/rapper-known-lil-zay-osama-sentenced-14-months-prison-possessing-illegal-machinegun" target="_blank" >sentenced<b> </b>him<b> </b>in 2024</a> to 14 months in prison after he pleaded guilty to possession of a machine gun. He left the pistol — affixed with a switch that turned it into an automatic weapon — in the back of a rideshare vehicle that took him from a luxury Manhattan hotel to a recording studio in Queens, prosecutors said.</p>
